Esek
EE-sek
proper noun
Hebrew 'eseq, “contention” or “strife,” from a root meaning to quarrel or press upon another; the name Isaac gave the first well the herdmen of Gerar strove for.

Biblical Definition

When Isaac’s servants digged in the valley of Gerar and found a well of springing water, the herdmen of Gerar strove with them, saying, The water is ours; and Isaac called the name of the well Esek, “Contention,” “because they strove with him” (Gen 26:20). Isaac had the right, for his father Abraham had digged those wells before him; yet the heir of promise did not stand upon his right nor answer strife with strife. He yielded the well and removed to dig again. Here is the meekness that inherits the earth, the temper the Lord blessed when He said, Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. The world reckons such yielding weakness; the covenant reckons it faith, for the man who trusts the LORD to make room for him need not seize a well by force. Esek stands as a monument to the peaceable heir who would rather lose a cistern than lose his peace, who overcomes not by contending but by giving place. In this Isaac was a son after the pattern of the greater Son, who, when He was reviled, reviled not again, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. The wells of the flesh are worth striving for only to the flesh; the child of promise digs, and if men take it, digs again, and waits upon the God who has wells enough.

Webster 1828 Definition

The first well Isaac digged in the valley of Gerar, named “Contention” because the herdmen of Gerar strove for it (Gen 26:20); a monument to the meek heir who yields his right rather than strive.

expand to see more

ESEK, a well in the valley of Gerar, the name signifying “contention.”

So called because the herdmen of Gerar strove with Isaac’s herdmen for the water (Gen 26:20).

Isaac held the right, yet yielded the well and removed to dig again.

A pattern of the meekness that inherits the earth and overcomes by giving place.

It stands over against Sitnah and Rehoboth as the first of Isaac’s three wells.

Key Scripture

Gen 26:20 — "And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him."

Gen 26:21 — "And they digged another well, and strove for that also: and he called the name of it Sitnah."

Gen 26:22 — "And he removed from thence, and digged another well; and for that they strove not: and he called the name of it Rehoboth; and he said, For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."

Gen 12:3 — "And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed."

Modern Corruption

The well of contention where Isaac yielded rather than strove; it recovers the meekness of faith that trusts God to make room.

expand to see more

Esek is a well in the wilderness of Gerar, and no man now disputes its memory as the herdmen once disputed its water. The name preserves a plain fact: Isaac had the right to the well, and Isaac gave it up rather than answer strife with strife.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the meekness that inherits the earth. The world counts yielding as weakness, but the covenant counts it faith; the man who trusts the LORD to make room need not seize a well by force. Learn of Isaac to give place, and of the greater Son who, when reviled, reviled not again.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew root meaning to contend, quarrel, or press upon; the noun names the strife itself.

expand to see more

Esek renders Hebrew 'eseq, “contention.”

The root 'asaq means to quarrel, contend, or press upon another.

The same root touches the idea of oppression and wrongful seizure.

Isaac fixed the sense by naming the well for the strife of the herdmen.

Kin in theme, though not in root, to Sitnah, “hatred,” the next well.

Usage

"Isaac called the first well Esek, because they strove with him."

"The strife of Esek did not move the patient heir to wrath."

"Every believer meets an Esek before he comes to his Rehoboth."
